Chapter 1: Arriving in a World Apart—First Impressions and Everyday Life
Imagine stepping off a plane in Pyongyang. The first thing you notice isn’t the quiet, but this almost tangible feeling that eyes are on you. The airport itself feels small, almost sleepy—and yet, the air is thick with anticipation.
Most of us know North Korea only through headlines or those blurry images on the news. But if you’re actually living and working here? Well, the reality’s a lot more complicated—and honestly, a lot more human—than any headline could ever show.
Those first few days? They’re a whirlwind of new routines. There’s always someone nearby—official minders, sometimes smiling, sometimes giving you that watchful look. And the city? It’s full of contrasts. You’ll see these wide, grand boulevards lined with massive monuments, but then you turn a corner and find a quiet park, with families picnicking and kids playing. The streets are almost spotless, but if you peek into the shops, shelves are pretty bare, and the lights can flicker on and off without warning.
To settle in, you’ve got to learn to pick up on what’s not being said. Conversations feel careful—every word chosen with care. At first, you might think people are distant. But after a while, you realize it’s just caution. Real trust? That grows slowly, over shared meals and those small, thoughtful gestures.
I’ll never forget the first time a local colleague invited me over. His apartment wasn’t fancy, but the welcome? That was genuine. His family served what they had—some rice, kimchi, a bit of meat saved for special moments. We laughed, swapped stories about the kids and their schoolwork, and even shared a few jokes about the constant power cuts. In moments like that, the rigid image of North Korea softens, and you see a society where people care deeply for their families and find joy in the little things.
Of course, you can’t escape the presence of the state. Every home has those portraits of the country’s leaders, and every conversation is shaped by what’s safe to say—and what’s not. It’s a reminder to stick to safe topics, steer clear of politics, and always respect the rules, both spoken and unspoken.
Getting around means learning the city’s unique rhythms. Buses and trams come and go on their own schedule, so most days, you’ll end up walking. The buildings are a mix—some grand, Soviet-style structures, others just plain, functional apartment blocks. And at dawn, you’ll see groups of workers out for collective exercises, moving together as music blares from loudspeakers—a scene that feels both carefully choreographed and yet, somehow, completely normal.
The hardest part for most people? That sense of being cut off. There’s barely any internet, international calls are rare, and news from outside arrives in tiny fragments. Even letters from home take weeks—if they make it at all. In this world, friendships with local colleagues become lifelines. They’re your bridge to connection and understanding.
Eventually, what felt strange at first starts to fade. You begin to appreciate just how resilient and resourceful people here are. Despite the constant challenges—like food shortages, power cuts, and always being watched—life keeps moving. Kids head off to school, couples get married, and neighbors look out for each other in quiet but powerful ways.
Living in North Korea teaches you to look beyond what’s on the surface. Sure, appearances matter here, but if you pay attention, you’ll find real warmth and humanity in unexpected places. So, maybe the most important lesson is this: nothing here is ever quite what it seems—and every single day brings a new surprise.
